preamble.text: Historical snapshot: later evidence may be reflected in current research pages and corrections.
Deterministically compiled from canonical evidence. Importance measures impact, not truth; evidence/confidence remain separate.

blocks.text: 1. DRYLAB-Bench reports elevated assay-based biosecurity risk scores in tool-augmented model evaluations

Desk: evaluation_science Evidence: A · credible_unconfirmed · active · importance 7/10 (Very major) Importance rationale: If replicated, evidence that frontier models can prioritize measured high-risk single-substitution designs and that a tool-augmented workflow raises assay-based scores could shift biosecurity evaluation and tool-access decisions across frontier AI programs. A 7 reflects cross-team significance while the preprint, assay-bounded proxy, single-substitution scope and unresolved workflow mechanism keep the claim short of a field-reset result.

What changed: A new preprint reports DRYLAB-Bench, an in-silico evaluation of biological-design outputs from 15 frontier language models across 30 policy-derived scenarios, scored against 187,695 pre-existing deep-mutational-scan measurements. The authors report that 67.6% of one-shot designs exceeded the average measured variant and 21.4% fell in the assay-specific highest-risk decile; under their tool-augmented iterative workflow, the top-decile share rose to 23.5% and the pooled Biosecurity Risk Score increased by 0.116 standard deviations. These are author-reported results from single-substitution assay proxies, not evidence of multi-variant organism-level outcomes, physical construction, or real-world harm. The paper’s sequential design does not isolate whether tool outputs or the additional deliberation cause the full increase, and no independent reproduction was inspected. Why it matters: If the reported assay-bounded results replicate, this evaluation moves biosecurity assessment beyond knowledge and refusal tests toward empirical measurement of model-generated designs and tool-augmented workflows. That could change how developers evaluate access to computational design tools. The measured single-substitution assay outcomes do not establish organism-level effects or operational threat.

Demonstrated: The inspected arXiv v1 paper documents the benchmark design and reports results for 15 frontier models across 30 scenarios. Those reported measurements have not been independently reproduced in this activation.

Claimed: Authors report that 67.6% of one-shot designs exceeded the average measured variant and 21.4% fell in the assay-specific top decile. In tool-augmented iterative conditions, they report a 23.5% top-decile share and a pooled Biosecurity Risk Score increase of +0.116 standard deviations.

Mechanism: The authors compare model-proposed single-substitution designs in one-shot and tool-augmented iterative settings, scoring them against pre-existing deep-mutational-scan measurements. The benchmark reports assay-relative risk proxies and does not perform biological synthesis.

Strongest baseline: The strongest within-paper baseline is the same model’s pre-tool one-shot submission in the same sequential trajectory. The authors also report single-round and repeated no-tool controls, but the no-tool iteration arm is under-sampled and noisy.

Regime: Author-run in-silico evaluation of 15 frontier models across 30 policy-derived scenarios, with scores mapped to 187,695 pre-existing ProteinGym/ViroGym single-substitution assay measurements. It does not measure multi-variant effects, host context, transmission or physical construction.

Limitations: Results are reported by the paper authors in a single preprint and were not independently reproduced in this activation.; The Biosecurity Risk Score is an assay-relative proxy based on single-substitution measurements; it does not establish multi-variant phenotypes, organism-level behavior, transmission or real-world harm.; The study’s sequential conditions do not fully separate tool-output effects from extra deliberation; the authors identify further controls that are not run.; The paper includes sensitive adversarial prompts and biological examples; this public record retains only high-level methods and aggregate results.

Open evidence gaps: No independent reproduction of the benchmark scoring, model runs or aggregate risk results was inspected.; The score is bounded to single-substitution assay measurements and does not establish multi-variant effects, host-context biology, transmission, or operational real-world risk.; The within-trajectory comparison does not isolate the causal contribution of tool-output content from extra deliberation; the paper describes two unrun mechanism controls.
Sources: https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.13116
2. A cryptographic construction illustrates a limit of elicitation-based model capability audits

Desk: evaluation_science Evidence: A · credible_unconfirmed · active · importance 7/10 (Very major) Importance rationale: If the construction and assumptions apply to realistic model supply chains, elicitation-based audits could fail against deliberately hidden computations, motivating complementary provenance and integrity controls. The paper’s empirical demonstration is small and does not establish prevalence in deployed models.

What changed: The paper constructs encrypted computations that can be embedded in model weights and conditionally hidden from polynomial-time elicitation under stated cryptographic assumptions. Its PyTorch proof of concept tests a small chemistry classifier: authors report resistance to supervised fine-tuning and latent adversarial training, while 8-bit gradient-based trigger search exhaustively enumerated 256 candidates and matched random search; the evaluated 16-bit query budget remained near chance. Correct-trigger chemistry accuracy was 73.5%. The authors report individual compiled GLU units in Gemma 3 270M and a separate small experiment using Gemma 4 E4B architecture, a 64-bit trigger and 12-round Keccak-p[1600]; they do not report a full evaluation in an actual pretrained checkpoint. The arXiv v2 record states acceptance at NeurIPS 2026. They also report raw compiled weights are anomalous, while obfuscation leaves possible within-layer correlation signals. This is a conditional construction and limited experiment, not evidence of hidden capabilities in deployed frontier models. Why it matters: The construction identifies a conditional limit for audits that rely on eliciting unwanted behavior, including white-box access, when an adversary can deliberately engineer model weights. It is a security result under cryptographic assumptions and a small proof-of-concept task, not evidence that deployed frontier models currently contain hidden dangerous capabilities.

Claimed: The authors report a cryptographically locked chemistry classifier resisted supervised fine-tuning, latent adversarial training and tested trigger search under the reported settings; their 8-bit trigger search exhaustively enumerated all 256 candidates and matched random search.

Mechanism: Encrypted neural networks are embedded in host weights and activated by a secret trigger; cryptographic assumptions support hardness of elicitation and interpretation even with weight access.

Strongest baseline: A separately trained password-locked classifier performs the same chemistry task but has a different correct-trigger accuracy (92.7% vs 73.5%). Random-network locker control shows no observed SFT/LAT benefit. The 8-bit trigger search enumerates all candidates, so it is not evidence that gradient search beats random search.

Regime: Cryptographic guarantee under the stated locker/security and compiler assumptions; empirical tests use a small 64-bit Morgan-fingerprint chemistry classifier, a 2.07-billion-parameter host construction, and three-run 95% confidence intervals for reported chemistry results.
Open evidence gaps: The paper’s proof and experiments have not been independently audited or reproduced; the full construction has not been integrated into a pretrained model.
Sources: https://arxiv.org/html/2610.13928
3. A mathematical-analysis preprint reports mismatches between OpenAI’s Navier-Stokes proof and cited Lean estimates

Desk: evaluation_science Evidence: A · credible_unconfirmed · active · importance 6/10 (Major) Importance rationale: If the reported mismatches hold, a machine-checked Lean result cannot be treated as verification of the specific natural-language proof without a semantic bridge. This changes how an extraordinary mathematical claim should be evaluated, although the audit does not refute the underlying theorem.

What changed: Bastounis, Circelli and Hansen compare OpenAI’s natural-language Navier–Stokes proof with cited Lean declarations. For Lemma 8.6, equation (8.19), they report that the manuscript states an m+4 derivative estimate while the cited Lean estimate requires m+5. For pressure-flux equation (10.19), they report a different Lean bound and proof route, including an additional localized gradient norm. They note one similar auxiliary bound in the repository does not appear to be directly used in the proposed theorem, leaving the effect on the actual proof dependency chain unresolved. The authors explicitly do not claim the natural-language blow-up proof is incorrect. This remains a source-reported critique in an arXiv preprint, without independent reproduction or established specialist consensus. Why it matters: A formal proof establishes its encoded theorem, but it does not by itself establish that the theorem matches the natural-language argument it is meant to check. The reported estimate differences give concrete targets for independent Lean and PDE review of an extraordinary mathematical claim, while leaving the truth of the underlying blow-up result unresolved.

Claimed: The authors report an m+4 versus m+5 derivative requirement in Lemma 8.6 and a distinct pressure-flux estimate/proof route for equation (10.19), challenging correspondence between selected manuscript arguments and cited Lean declarations.

Mechanism: Compares selected estimates and proof steps in OpenAI’s natural-language Navier–Stokes paper against cited Lean declarations and pinned source revisions. The critique separates encoded theorem validity from semantic fidelity to the written argument.

Strongest baseline: OpenAI’s natural-language paper and its cited Lean declarations are compared directly. The authors report explicit estimate differences but do not claim the natural-language theorem is false; neither the critique nor theorem has independent peer-reviewed resolution in this review.
Regime: Selected analytic estimates in one natural-language Navier-Stokes proof and corresponding Lean declarations; the paper does not audit every proof dependency or disprove the theorem.

Limitations: This is an author-reported analysis in an arXiv v1 preprint; peer review and independent specialist consensus were not established.; The paper compares selected proof components and cited Lean declarations; it does not establish that the underlying Navier–Stokes blow-up theorem is false.; For Lemma 8.6, the authors identify a specific m+4 versus m+5 derivative requirement in the manuscript and cited Lean estimate. For pressure-flux equation (10.19), they report a different bound involving localized gradient norm A_R. They also note one similar auxiliary estimate is not directly used in the proposed theorem; impact on the complete theorem dependency path remains unresolved.; No independent reproduction of the reported estimate comparison or audit of later upstream revisions was performed.

Open evidence gaps: No independent reproduction of the reported m+4/m+5 or pressure-flux estimate comparisons, and no reconciliation against later OpenAI repository revisions, were completed as of this review.; The preprint does not refute the underlying blow-up theorem. It reports selected formal correspondence gaps; the effect on the theorem’s actual proof dependencies remains unresolved, especially because the authors note one similar auxiliary bound is not directly used in the theorem.
Sources: https://arxiv.org/html/2610.08144v1
4. ReAgent reports improved paper–repository consistency audits on one research-agent benchmark

Desk: evaluation_science Evidence: A · credible_unconfirmed · active · importance 6/10 (Major) Importance rationale: If automated checks can detect when research claims diverge from their code and execution artifacts, they could improve auditability as agents produce more research outputs. The evidence is one author-evaluated benchmark on an auditable subset and does not establish scientific validity or broad generalization.

What changed: ReAgent combines static inspection of paper claims against repository implementations with dynamic execution evidence. On 96 auditable repositories from a screened set of 188 AutoSOTA agent-generated paper–repository pairs, the authors report 70.83% overall audit accuracy versus 35.42% for Codex using GPT-5.4 and manually established ground truth. Ninety-two repositories were excluded, mostly because datasets or checkpoints were unavailable. The result is author-reported and limited to one platform. Why it matters: As research agents generate papers, code and experiments together, an audit that checks both implementation fidelity and execution evidence could catch unsupported claims that either static review or successful reproduction alone misses. This benchmark concerns artifact consistency; it does not certify whether a method or conclusion is scientifically valid.

Claimed: Among 96 auditable AutoSOTA repositories, the authors report 70.83% overall audit accuracy versus 35.42% for Codex. Dynamic verification accuracy is reported as 90.63%; 33 repositories reproduced their reported metrics, but only 25 passed both static consistency and reproduction.

Mechanism: Static verification extracts claim contracts and aligns them with implementation evidence; dynamic verification plans and runs experiments, records execution traces, and distinguishes matched, mismatched, blocked and not-reproduced outcomes.
Strongest baseline: Codex using the same GPT-5.4 model and task inputs; the paper reports 35.42% overall audit accuracy versus ReAgent’s 70.83%.

Regime: A manually audited, auditable subset of AutoSOTA: 96 of 188 agent-generated paper–repository pairs. Ninety-two were excluded, mostly for unavailable datasets or checkpoints. Evaluation used manually established ground truth and GPT-5.4 across compared methods.
Open evidence gaps: The reported benchmark comparison has not been independently reproduced.; Generalization beyond the AutoSOTA repository collection is unknown.
Sources: https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.22111
5. Et Tu, Brute? reports wealth-conditioned recommendations by personal AI agents

Desk: policy_geopolitics Evidence: A · credible_unconfirmed · active · importance 6/10 (Major) Importance rationale: If replicated, agents that condition recommendations on inferred wealth even against explicit cost goals could create a consequential objective-following and economic-discrimination risk in personal-agent deployments. The current evidence is a synthetic benchmark suite, not observed field prevalence or intentional pricing behavior.

What changed: In a September 2026 preprint revised to v2 on September 25, authors report 325,000 experiments across 13 personal-agent configurations and three decisions: flights, health insurance and graduate programs. Eight models systematically recommend more expensive options to wealthier users under otherwise identical requests. The reported effect can persist against an explicit cheapest-option request and when wealth is inferred from task-unrelated email; the authors describe this as benchmark evidence of wealth-conditioned recommendations, not evidence of intent or field prevalence. Why it matters: Personal agents use private context to personalize decisions, but incidental attributes can shape choices against explicit objectives. The paper offers controlled evidence that inferred socioeconomic status may change recommendations in some models and domains, a mechanism worth testing in agent architecture and product evaluations. It does not show intentional exploitation, real-world incidence or that every model behaves this way.
Demonstrated: The arXiv preprint and its method/experimental design were inspected. The numerical outcome is reported by the paper authors and is not independently demonstrated in this review.

Claimed: Across 325,000 author-run experiments, 13 agents and three consumer decision domains, authors report that 8 models choose more expensive options for wealthier users under otherwise identical requests. Some continue to do so when asked for the cheapest option or when wealth is inferred from unrelated email; blocking other attributes can leave disparity unchanged or increase it by up to 40% in insurance. Claude Opus 4.8 has the largest reported effect in this benchmark.

Mechanism: Authors compare recommendations across profile and inbox context conditions while holding user requests constant, vary which attributes are withheld, and measure price and quality characteristics of recommended flights, insurance and graduate programs. They report that blocking direct financial attributes can leave proxy-based inference available.

Strongest baseline: Same decision requests under zero-context and varied profile/inbox conditions; price and quality of recommendations are compared across inferred-wealth groups. No field deployment or independent replication.

Regime: Author-run adversarial-delegation benchmark using flight, health-insurance and graduate-program decisions with profile and email context conditions; 13 agents, 8 models as described in the paper; model versions and synthetic task construction limit transfer to field behavior.

Limitations: All results are author-reported benchmark outcomes; no independent reproduction or field study was inspected.; Eight of thirteen models show the reported systematic behavior, so the result is not universal across tested agents.; Recommendation disparities do not establish intentional exploitation, actual transaction prices or population-level consumer harm.; The three benchmark domains and profile/email construction do not establish behavior across all personal-agent tasks, deployed products or current model versions.; Attribute blocking can change what information is available and may induce proxy substitution; privacy redaction alone does not establish preference alignment.

Open evidence gaps: No independent reproduction of the 325,000-experiment benchmark or its model/version conditions was inspected.; No field-prevalence or hard-constraint intervention study was inspected.
Sources: https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.24927
6. Alibaba announces 5–10T Qwen roadmap, V900 accelerator and 2032 cloud-capacity target

Desk: labs_industry Evidence: A · credible_unconfirmed · active · importance 6/10 (Major) Importance rationale: If delivered, coordinating a 5–10T model roadmap, a domestically designed accelerator and a >20 GW operated capacity target could materially affect a major AI engineering and infrastructure program. The record is a company roadmap with unverified performance and future execution, which limits the consequence assessment to major rather than field-shifting.

What changed: In a September 25, 2026 Chinese-language company report about its 2026 Cloud栖 Conference, Alibaba said Qwen 4 was in training and gave a roadmap for Qwen 4.5 and Qwen 5 to scale to 5–10 trillion parameters. It described its Zhenwu V900 accelerator as up to three times the performance of M890, with 216 GB memory and 1,200 GB/s interconnect bandwidth, and said mass production and market launch were planned for 2027 Q1. Alibaba also set a target for Alibaba Cloud-operated global data-center capacity to exceed 20 GW by 2032. These are company-reported plans and specifications; independent model, chip-performance and capacity evidence was not inspected. Why it matters: If executed, the linked model, accelerator and infrastructure roadmap could materially affect Alibaba’s ability to scale AI training and cloud inference. The reviewed evidence supports an ambitious company plan, not completed delivery or measured performance.
Demonstrated: The company report documents that Alibaba announced these roadmap and specification claims. No delivered model/chip performance is established.
Claimed: Alibaba reports a Qwen 4.5/Qwen 5 roadmap at 5–10T parameters and a planned V900 accelerator with up-to-3x M890 performance.

Mechanism: The announcement links future model development, a T-Head AI accelerator and Alibaba Cloud-operated data-center expansion. This is strategic coupling stated by the company; integration outcomes are unmeasured.

Strongest baseline: The company compares V900 with its predecessor M890 and projects future model/capacity scale; the inspected report supplies neither benchmark conditions nor independently verified baseline and delivery data.
Regime: Alibaba’s announced Qwen roadmap, T-Head V900 accelerator schedule/specification and Alibaba Cloud global capacity target, as described in the company’s 2026 conference report.

Limitations: All technical specifications, performance comparisons, roadmap dates and capacity targets are attributed company statements in one company report.; The up-to-3x comparison has no stated workload or test method in the inspected report; it cannot establish general accelerator performance or competitiveness.; No conclusion is made about realized model scale, model quality, chip shipments, customer adoption, facility construction, operating capacity, power procurement or economic returns.; Reuters’ September 22 report was rate-limited in this review and is not treated as inspected corroboration.

Open evidence gaps: The V900 comparison is not tied to a named model, precision, throughput/latency, power, workload, test harness or independently checked result in the inspected report.; The future 5–10T model-series roadmap lacks a technical report, architecture/active-parameter definition, training status beyond Qwen 4, evaluation regime and release schedule.; No independently verified baseline, accounting boundary, interim milestones, power availability or completed construction evidence was inspected for the >20 GW 2032 capacity target.
Sources: https://www.alibabagroup.com/zh-CN/document-2041268239081668608
agents_memory

items: Feedback coding reports reliable black-box covert messages in bounded LLM tests — importance 5/10 · The paper introduces Burnashev Adaptive Posterior Matching (BAM), which uses transcript feedback, posterior matching and a confirmation phase to embed messages in generated text without giving the receiver the model’s weights or prompt. On C4 RealNews, the authors report roughly 0–0.1% error for an 8-bit payload in about 46–50 tokens across three open-weight models and 1,000 trials, versus roughly 10.5–16.8% for the strongest listed black-box baseline at 50 tokens. In separate conversational experiments, error varied by model and task: Llama-3.1 and Phi-4 stayed below 3% message error, while Qwen3-A3B-30B had 19–22% dialogue error. These are one preprint’s results; no independent reproduction was found, the implementation has computational costs, and transcript editing is outside the stated security model. — FCMO-DFB3BC914F13

RoboTalk trains compact vision-language models for explicit multi-robot coordination in simulation — importance 5/10 · The revised preprint reports 7,950 FSM-validated synthetic trajectories for 53 RoboCasa-derived kitchen tasks. In closed-loop simulation, Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct reaches 65% success on 10 held-out tasks; adding rationale targets to the Thinking model reports up to 77%. These are author-reported simulator results, not physical-robot tests. — FCMO-19BFDD9D0FE6

A paper models how distractor growth can weaken evidence retrieval in long-context models — importance 5/10 · The authors formalize “context poisoning” as competition between a decisive evidence score and the maximum score among distractors. Under a softmax retrieval abstraction, they derive a finite-sample bound in which the evidence margin needed to hold accuracy above base rate grows as Ω(√log N), where N is the effective distractor count. Controlled experiments report decreasing retrieval accuracy as context grows with hard negatives; same-format distractors produce the largest drop among the tested constructions, while retrieval gating helps only when evidence recall is preserved. — FCMO-10A013EEF5C3

PhysAI-Bench reports a 52% best score on trace-derived UAV decisions — importance 5/10 · The authors present PhysAI-Bench, a multiple-choice benchmark for foundation-model action selection from trace-derived autonomous UAV missions. Its repository describes 10,178 decisions with four candidate actions, a 35-instance human-verified development set and a 500-instance episode-disjoint held-out set. After selecting a model-specific prompt and temperature configuration, the authors report GPT-5.3 Chat at 52.00% held-out decision accuracy, the highest listed score. The reference answer is the action taken in the original mission, not necessarily the only valid or globally optimal action. The repository lists the full dataset, locked split manifests, evaluation code and model outputs as release-pending. — FCMO-1F6BBDBD11C9

ActGov reports benchmark reductions in indirect prompt-injection success through per-action authorization checks — importance 5/10 · A September 2026 preprint introduces ActGov, which checks each proposed tool call against a task-scoped policy before execution. The authors report lower indirect prompt-injection success on AgentDojo and AgentDyn across four model backends, with task utility retained to varying degrees. Their cross-domain transfer test also shows severe over-restriction: an AgentDojo-trained policy has 0.100 clean-task utility on AgentDyn versus 0.767 without defense. These are paper-reported benchmark results, not independent reproduction or evidence of deployment effectiveness. — FCMO-08FB79207C91

A preprint reports that separating environmental facts from task procedures can help evolving agents — importance 5/10 · A September 21, 2026 arXiv preprint proposes TTSE, which evolves environmental facts (FACT) separately from task-conditioned procedures (TIP), using interaction evidence to revise or retire both kinds of rule. The paper frames representation errors and execution errors as distinct contributors to agent failure and evaluates the framework on ALFWorld, ScienceWorld, GDPevo, SOPBench and PinchBench. Authors report gains over selected baselines and an end-to-end PinchBench score of 0.7822 versus 0.7439 across three runs. In the SOPBench comparison, the reported dual-track gain over a single-track Bayesian-memory ablation is 2.99 percentage points over 892 tasks, but warehouse inspection contributes 78% of the gain; without that domain the reported gap is 0.67 points, and dangerous-goods tasks slightly favor single-track. The preprint reports no independent reproduction; its GDPevo dual-versus-TIP ablation is not formally significance-tested, and induced rules lack a structured verification gate. — FCMO-26608BE50499

Loopjacking paper reports agent approval reused for materially changed operations in tested product paths — importance 5/10 · A September 2026 preprint defines Loopjacking as product logic applying a human decision for an operation A to a materially different operation B. In purposively selected tests, the author reports post-approval substitution in seven sampled Agno AgentOS releases and 12 sampled in-memory LangGraph Agent Server compositions with a declared authorization policy, plus an incomplete shell-command approval representation in OpenClaw 2026.2.23. OpenClaw 2026.2.24 rejected the tested mismatch. OpenAI Agents SDK 0.22.0 and 0.22.2 served as negative controls that rejected same-call mutation. The tests used synthetic principals and harmless recording sinks; they do not estimate prevalence, establish user susceptibility, or show all versions are affected. — FCMO-21277C154D52

CICL reports improved first-file retrieval from decision-aware reranking on a small coding benchmark — importance 4/10 · The v4 preprint presents the Counterfactual-Inspired Context Layer (CICL), which ranks candidate repository evidence by estimated effect on an agent’s next action and can compress selected context into typed memory cards. On 50 SWE-bench Verified file-retrieval instances, the authors report that Qwen3.6-Plus reranking of BM25 top-50 candidates raises hit@1 from 0.58 to 0.78 and MRR@10 from 0.634 to 0.790. Top-10 recall is 0.714 versus 0.716, and the result measures file retrieval rather than patch success. The paper’s own terminology is counterfactual-inspired; it does not claim formal causal identification. — FCMO-731B1BCA417D

RegimeAbstain estimates multi-hop retrieval failure from query and ANN structure — importance 4/10 · The September 2026 RegimeAbstain preprint models retrieval confidence from query and approximate-nearest-neighbor structure, without an extra language-model call, then abstains on risky multi-hop retrievals. Across three benchmarks and two retrieval architectures, the authors report confident-wrong-answer rates of 14.5%–62.1%. On MuSiQue with an LLM-judge pipeline, they report reducing that rate from 39.5% to 20.6% at 50% coverage, with expected calibration error 0.035. — FCMO-88769E567A1C

AutoViewMem organizes long-term conversational memory into learned semantic views — importance 4/10 · The September 2026 AutoViewMem preprint proposes learning low-overlap semantic views from conversational traces and using them to structure memory at write time, followed by offline consolidation and ordinary top-K retrieval. The authors report improved long-horizon question answering and personalization over memory baselines on LoCoMo and PersonaMem with Qwen3-8B and Qwen3-14B. — FCMO-856F53F93E55

MemCalib measures whether language-model agents give stored facts the right influence — importance 4/10 · An October 8 v3 preprint introduces MemCalib, a benchmark that scores whether each fact in an agent’s stored memory should be ignored, used as bounded support, or allowed to control the answer. The authors report 15,000 examples across health, general assistance and coding. On its 1,500-example test set, the highest listed exact calibration is 28.40% for GPT-5.6-SOL; most evaluated models more often over-use memory than under-use it. The authors report that MemCalib-RL improves Qwen3-8B atom-use accuracy on this benchmark and transfers to a 150-query RPEval subset, while increasing under-use relative to the base model. Results are paper-reported and rely on constructed memory examples and rubric-guided model judging; real-world transfer is unknown. — FCMO-2855FF416D32

items: Complex KDA extends Kimi Delta Attention state-transition expressivity — importance 5/10 · Complex KDA (CKDA) combines two parameter-range extensions—signed channel gates and a delta coefficient up to 2—to make Kimi Delta Attention express 2D rotations using a single diagonal-plus-rank-one recurrent transition. The paper proves exact representability for orthogonal diagonal-plus-rank-one matrices and reports finite-group state-tracking, synthetic periodic-audio and language-model experiments. The authors report stronger length extrapolation on selected synthetic tasks and language-model results comparable to KDA, not a broad demonstrated language-model advantage. Open code and committed measurements aid inspection; no independent proof audit or training reproduction was conducted. — FCMO-ED9251AD04F0

CS-MoE reports cross-layer expert sharing with matched-budget perplexity gains through 12B parameters — importance 4/10 · A preprint proposes CS-MoE, which combines layer-local experts with a shared expert pool available across transformer layers. The authors report lower perplexity than dense and layer-isolated MoE baselines under matched parameter and FLOP budgets in Qwen3-backbone experiments spanning 0.6B–12B parameters. At 8B scale, one reported configuration activates 55% of physical parameters per forward pass and reaches perplexity 9.55 versus 9.75 for the dense baseline; this result is not the same as the paper’s separate 4.5-trillion-token downstream comparison. The largest reported models are 12B; routing stability, distributed-system efficiency, and post-training behavior at larger scales remain unestablished. — FCMO-996A9DA8F42A

For Lemma 8.6, equation (8.19), they report that the manuscript states an m+4 derivative estimate while the cited Lean estimate requires m+5. On 96 auditable repositories from a screened set of 188 AutoSOTA agent-generated paper–repository pairs, the authors report 70.83% overall audit accuracy versus 35.42% for Codex using GPT-5.4 and manually established ground truth. MMSafe reports multilingual fine-tuning filter that lowers measured safety regressions — importance 5/10 · A preprint proposes MMSafe, which scores fine-tuning examples using both a language-shared safety-sensitive layer and language-specific layers. Across four Llama and Qwen model variants, two fine-tuning datasets and three multilingual safety benchmarks, the authors report harmful-response ratios averaging about 39% of random-filtering baselines; the method beats a prior single-layer filter on three of four model variants. They report that general and multilingual utility scores remain broadly similar in the tested settings, but results vary by dataset, model and language-specific weighting. Findings are limited to the paper’s LoRA fine-tuning and benchmark settings. The authors report releasing code, but this activation did not run it or independently reproduce the results. — FCMO-266232F3118E

Repeated materials campaigns report a shared frontier and a common-mode structure error — importance 5/10 · A preprint compares 16 one-week autonomous materials-discovery campaigns given the same 12,499-entry metal-organic-framework database, methane-storage objective and pinned protocol. The authors report divergent search strategies but convergence near 200 cm³/cm³, with an independent calculation placing its nine best structures among agent reports. However, 15 of 16 campaigns also selected an audit-excluded incomplete structure whose missing anions created artificial pore volume. Enforced checks improved fresh-run reproduction from 1/8 to 8/8 in the tested subset but did not detectably improve conclusion validity. — FCMO-08BCA3190169

OSWorld-Pro adds process-level diagnostics to computer-use evaluation — importance 5/10 · The September 2026 OSWorld-Pro preprint introduces a process-based benchmark for computer-use agents with more than 300 tasks, 2,800 sequential subgoals and over 67,000 human annotations. Authors use human-aligned language-model judges to score subgoal fulfillment through trajectories. They report Claude Opus 5 at 75.7% on OSWorld-Pro versus 83.4% on OSWorld and identify failure patterns such as irrelevant actions and click mistakes. — FCMO-6E05AB159B0A

Available Guardrails quantifies when selective prediction can be certified — importance 5/10 · The September 2026 Available Guardrails preprint studies whether finite calibration data can certify target precision for every reporting unit in a selective prediction system. It uses exact-binomial inversion and dynamic programming to expose the trade-off among certified precision, subgroup granularity and served traffic. In author-run evaluations, split-sample partition selection gains a reported mean 0.060 coverage over support balancing, with a positive direction in 59 of 60 model effects across three intent-routing datasets and two architectures; a naive estimator captures only 0.005 of a reported 0.157 population-known opportunity. — FCMO-CA2F66E7D798

BabelArena tests agent execution across 23 languages and reports resource-linked failure gaps — importance 5/10 · A September 20 preprint introduces BabelFlow, a workflow for adapting agent benchmarks across languages while preserving links among prompts, tools, environments and evaluators, and releases BabelArena with 16,146 instances across 23 languages. In a 40-task Chinese ablation, the authors report fewer broken references and behavioral mismatches than independent translation, at higher token cost. Their five-model evaluation reports lower task success and language consistency in the low-resource language group, with distinct tool-use/control-flow failures and increased input-token use in sampled tasks. These are paper-reported findings; translation validity, independent reproduction and generalization remain open. — FCMO-FB444CC0F9E4

A systematic review maps specification, verification, and enforcement gaps in LLM agent safety — importance 5/10 · A June 2026 preprint surveys safety methods for LLM agents that take multi-step actions. The authors report a PRISMA 2020 review of 38 studies and organize the field around specification, verification, and enforcement. Their synthesis identifies errors in translating natural-language requirements into formal rules as a major bottleneck and notes that action-level blocking does not necessarily yield safe task completion. The strongest verifier-tax result comes from one study of tau-bench Airline/Retail tasks: in that study, per-proposal interception reached 94.1% in one setting while safe-success rates were below 5% in most tested configurations; the authors also report 2.0–2.8× token inflation for their Triad architectures. The study used two open-weight models, different 15/30-turn caps, and an unseeded stochastic user simulator, and has no independent reproduction identified. The survey itself was unregistered and conducted by a single reviewer without an inter-rater check, so it is useful field orientation rather than a settled comparative assessment. — FCMO-C675AE392767

SpecOpt reports residue-aware optimization of predicted molecular selectivity — importance 4/10 · The preprint proposes optimizing ligand specificity by contrasting predicted residue contacts for a target and up to three off-target proteins. On a 915-compound ChEMBL-derived benchmark, the authors report that 776 compounds (84.8%) improved the target-minus-off-target AutoDock Vina score gap, with the mean changing from −0.718 to +0.472 kcal/mol and mean Tanimoto similarity of 0.72 to the starting molecules. The reported results are docking scores, not measured binding or experimental selectivity. — FCMO-168348722EE2

A survey of a literature-review agent reports stated trust despite mandatory checkpoints — importance 4/10 · A preprint evaluates CoSLR, a multi-agent system for systematic literature reviews with retrieval grounding and mandatory human checkpoints. In a remote, self-paced survey study, 63 participants completed a simplified workflow in about 15 minutes; recruitment used convenience channels and participants were mainly from software engineering. The authors report that 22/63 (34.9%) rated their trust in generated summaries and reports at 4 or 5 on a five-point scale for acceptance without additional checking after brief interaction. They also report that 27/63 (42.9%) rated usability highly. These are post-interaction self-reports: the study did not observe full reviews or whether participants actually skipped verification. — FCMO-D70612FA5E90

blocks.text: inference_systems

items: StateMem reports persistent task memory and adaptive VLA caching gains in simulation and robot tests — importance 5/10 · StateMem adds a persistent single-token memory to a vision-language-action policy: prediction-error residuals update task state, while an adaptive router reuses cached VLM prefixes and applies a correction branch. The paper reports 97.6% average success on LIBERO, 20.25% fewer prefix refreshes than full refresh, and 26.8% task success / 44.4% cumulative success on RoboMemArena among the compared single-VLA methods. Across six real-world tasks and 20 trials each on one xArm7 platform, it reports 65% average success versus 44% for π0.5 and 53% for a MemoryVLA reimplementation. Efficiency gains depend on workload: LIBERO latency falls from 156.36 to 150.78 ms, while high refresh on RoboMemArena makes routing slower than full refresh. Training used four RTX A6000 GPUs for about five days. These are author-run results, not independent validation; one-token memory and one embodiment limit transfer. — FCMO-7BB77058887F

Cisco reports cross-vendor H200/MI350X inference above standalone throughput sum — importance 5/10 · Cisco's September 21, 2026 report describes an MLPerf Inference v6.1 GPT-OSS 120B Server submission that split prefill across eight NVIDIA H200 GPUs and decode across eight AMD Instinct MI350X GPUs over a Cisco Ethernet fabric. Cisco reports 70,085.48 tokens/s as the arithmetic sum of separately measured system throughputs and 73,357.62 tokens/s when combined (104.7% of that sum), while meeting applicable p99 TTFT and TPOT limits. MLCommons separately identifies Cisco as the first cross-vendor heterogeneous accelerator submission. The accessible MLCommons summary does not repeat Cisco's exact throughput figures, and the official raw workbook was not retrievable in this review; the numeric performance comparison therefore remains attributed to Cisco. — FCMO-74BC07BAE9B0

LumoTree reports modest replay gains for speculative verification on a hybrid language model — importance 4/10 · The LumoTree v3 preprint combines path-parallel tree verification with accepted-path state replay for a recurrent-hybrid language model. On 43 fixed recorded requests, the authors report 28.13 pooled tokens/s across three runs, compared with 26.12 for five-token native multi-token prediction (MTP). In a separate 10-task coding-agent study, one attempt per arm resolved five tasks with LumoTree versus six with MTP-5, and the LumoTree arm took longer in aggregate. The paper does not claim task-completion speedup; the replay result is specific to its GB10 serving setup and small corpora. — FCMO-AACA8CBEB134

blocks.text: labs_industry

items: Alibaba announces 5–10T Qwen roadmap, V900 accelerator and 2032 cloud-capacity target — importance 6/10 · In a September 25, 2026 Chinese-language company report about its 2026 Cloud栖 Conference, Alibaba said Qwen 4 was in training and gave a roadmap for Qwen 4.5 and Qwen 5 to scale to 5–10 trillion parameters. It described its Zhenwu V900 accelerator as up to three times the performance of M890, with 216 GB memory and 1,200 GB/s interconnect bandwidth, and said mass production and market launch were planned for 2027 Q1. Alibaba also set a target for Alibaba Cloud-operated global data-center capacity to exceed 20 GW by 2032. These are company-reported plans and specifications; independent model, chip-performance and capacity evidence was not inspected. — FCMO-0A73897EC6A8

IFR reports about 7,000 full-size humanoid sales in 2025, with a non-projected supplier sample — importance 5/10 · The International Federation of Robotics reports about 7,000 sales of full-size humanoid robots above 140 cm worldwide in 2025. Its release says current uses remain specialized and often involve human teleoperation, while its presentation says the segment is still moving from laboratories to pilots. This is an industry-reported statistic, not an independently verified census: the IFR says its World Robotics service-robot figures use a 238-company sample, are not projected to the whole industry, and vary in sample composition each year. — FCMO-EA1A6770B904

blocks.text: multimodality_world_models

items: DexTacWAM reports higher scores when tactile contact is modeled as part of the robot’s predicted world state — importance 5/10 · DexTacWAM treats fingertip tactile dynamics as part of a robot’s predicted world state rather than only as an extra policy input. It encodes each finger, compresses five tactile streams into one hand-level representation, and jointly predicts visual and tactile futures for action generation. On six contact-rich real-robot tasks, the authors report mean score 70.6 versus 38.0 for the strongest listed baseline over 20 trials per method/task. A four-task ablation reports a drop from 74.7 to 26.6 when tactile world modeling is removed while keeping tactile features and action expert. The paper also reports four hours of tactile-encoder adaptation, about 100 demonstrations per task, retention of visual prediction within 0.5 dB, and faster training/inference with compression. These are author-run results on one 22-DoF platform; camera access is matched, but the method’s relative end-effector actions differ from baseline action parameterizations, and no independent reproduction was located. — FCMO-64B30DCEA7C5

VideoXAgent reports competitive long-video results with query-driven expert tools — importance 5/10 · A September 11 preprint introduces VideoXAgent, an online harness that decomposes a video question and invokes specialized tools such as detection, OCR, speech recognition and frame inspection as needed. The authors report competitive performance on Video-MME-Long, LongVideoBench-Long, LVBench and MINERVA; on MINERVA they report 65.7% accuracy and about 15% of the context footprint of a 1,024-frame dense-packing baseline. The paper says its efficiency measure counts retrieved evidence and maximum agent context, not total token cost. These are author-reported benchmark results; the review did not run the system or independently reproduce them. — FCMO-065343B22606

Pelican-Sim pairs numeric robot actions with rendered motion cues and reports downstream gains in RoboTwin — importance 5/10 · A September 10 technical report from the Beijing Innovation Center of Humanoid Robotics describes Pelican-Sim 1.0, an action-conditioned video world model that combines a 28-dimensional robot-configuration vector with camera-aligned, URDF-rendered arm-motion cues, sparse mixture-of-experts layers and a distilled four-step rollout model. The authors report improved video-prediction metrics over evaluated baselines on AgiBotWorld Beta, RoboMIND and RoboTwin. In RoboTwin randomized tests, augmenting 10, 30 or 50 demonstrations per task with ten generated trajectories per demonstration raised policy success from 28.5% to 64.5%, 57.0% to 87.0%, and 70.0% to 93.0%, respectively, over five tasks and 200 unseen seeds per task. A world-model-plus-VLM evaluator reportedly ranked five policy checkpoints with Pearson correlation 0.994 after 1,000 task-specific adaptation rollouts; the test replayed the same action trajectories in the world model and simulator. The results are author-reported and primarily simulation-bounded. They do not establish physical-robot policy improvement, independent replication, or reliable closed-loop deployment under model-generated observations. — FCMO-4E24886E7375

VLM-in-Sandbox reports bounded visual evidence state for multimodal agents — importance 5/10 · The preprint presents a training-free visual workspace that registers sandbox-generated images in a ledger, keeps active visual context bounded and lets the model choose which artifacts to re-inspect. Across seven benchmarks, the authors report a 2.52 percentage-point pooled accuracy gain for GPT-4.1-mini over an append-only sandbox on 6,350 examples (95% CI 1.83–3.21), with 302 rescues and 142 regressions. A compiler-matched study on 1,260 examples reports 66.27% accuracy with 18.6% fewer total tokens than an automatic retain-all control. These are author-reported results, with heterogeneous per-benchmark effects and no independent reproduction. — FCMO-EF3E15D8EB31

THAW-VLA distills world-model features into a compact robot policy — importance 5/10 · THAW-VLA uses a frozen world model to produce cached training-frame features, then adds a feature-alignment loss to a compact vision-language-action policy. The teacher and projector are removed before deployment, so inference uses the undistilled student graph. The authors report a 0.8B policy moving from 95.3% to 97.9% mean success on LIBERO and from 48.2% to 50.5% on RoboCasa-GR1; they also report gains over the same student on single-arm and bimanual real-robot tasks, with 30 trials per cell. A single RTX 5090 profile is reported at 32 ms and 1.86 GB. Results remain author-reported and task-specific; independent reproduction and broader robot/task coverage are open. — FCMO-6B232DEBE030

A compositional benchmark exposes the reuse–forgetting tradeoff in continual robot world models — importance 5/10 · A September 18, 2026 arXiv preprint introduces a benchmark for continual world models in robot manipulation. Six simulated task curricula end with compositions of earlier action and perception primitives, separating reuse on a new task from forgetting on earlier tasks. The authors evaluate DreamerV3 and TD-MPC2 with fine-tuning, replay, EWC and PackNet, plus a modular Prismatic World Model. In a diagnostic with an encoder pretrained on demonstrations from all benchmark tasks and then frozen, PWM reports mean forgetting score 3.85 and forward-transfer score 36.18 across six suites, compared with 34.97 and 38.11 for TD-MPC2 using that same encoder; lower forgetting and higher forward transfer are better. Without this privileged encoder, PWM is reported on par with TD-MPC2. The study is limited to simulation, three seeds, selected model settings, and no controlled parameter or compute budgets; it does not establish physical-robot performance. — FCMO-52772AF29E99

A preprint reports that persistent spatial guidance improved object acquisition in a small blind-user study — importance 5/10 · A September 18, 2026 arXiv preprint describes Touvigation, a phone-based assistive object-acquisition system that combines vision-language interpretation with persistent local 3D tracking. Its audio guidance shifts from room-scale orientation and step counts to body-relative reaching cues and tactile verification. In a within-subject study, the authors report 48 successful trials out of 48 with Touvigation, versus 28/48 with ByteDance's Doubao assistant and 41/48 without AI; they also report faster completion and lower workload. The finding is bounded to 12 blind adults, two unfamiliar rooms and short-term use after familiarization. Participants were from one regional community and one severity category; the system depends on a LiDAR-equipped chest-mounted iPhone, initial room scanning, stable tracking and cloud processing. The study has not been independently replicated. — FCMO-1860A797BCC3

A preprint reports label-free visual grounding gains at inference, but not from pilot distillation — importance 5/10 · A September 21, 2026 arXiv preprint evaluates a model's sensitivity to question-relevant image crops as a label-free visual-evidence signal. On one 191-example V*Bench evaluation using three Qwen vision-language models, the authors report that selecting among 16 candidate crops raised fine-grained answer accuracy from about 70% to 85% and localized target regions 4.4–5.1 times above chance. Combining the evidence-gap signal with model confidence improved correctness prediction in the reported test. The authors also tested gated self-distillation: on HR-Bench, no gating, trajectory gating and token gating all scored below the base model, with more aggressive gating performing worse. The inference and training findings come from different tests and should remain separate. Results are author-reported, unreproduced and limited to one small benchmark; the crop search also requires 16 forward passes per example. — FCMO-8CF914FD8C2A

A preprint reports GPT-6 Astra leading a simulated robot benchmark, with sharp control limits — importance 5/10 · A September 21, 2026 arXiv preprint reports an evaluation of GPT-6 Astra acting directly as a robot manipulation policy, without task-specific fine-tuning or a learned motor policy in the control path. Across 42 RoboDojo simulation tasks and 2,100 trials, the authors report 22.48% average success and a score of 28.97, above the 40 public policies in their September 10 leaderboard snapshot. The result is uneven: Astra trails the top policy on precision, long-horizon and memory axes, while GPT-5.5 and DeepSeek-Flash perform much worse in the same reported interface. The authors say they stopped real-robot trials after unsafe actions damaged equipment; the paper does not establish real-world reliability or safe control. These are preprint-reported results without independent reproduction, and the public-policy runs did not receive the wiki-derived task text supplied to the LLMs. — FCMO-CA4E3C495479

INSPECT learns robot inspection views from assembly-assistant records — importance 5/10 · A September 2026 preprint introduces INSPECT, which learns robot view preferences from egocentric assembly-assistant records by separating evidence needed to resolve a claim from observation changes a robot camera can reproduce, then calibrating relative views to robot pose. In offline fixed-lattice replay on gearbox assemblies, the authors report mean human-rated view utility of 1.205 and full verifiability of 41.7% across 132 matched trials, versus 1.045 and 34.8% for the current-view baseline. On 1,068 IMPACT trials, its relative-view selector reports a 54.3% correct-decision rate versus 50.6% for current view. These are author-reported results in two constrained replay settings, not a live closed-loop deployment or independent reproduction. — FCMO-5A6AA5C74732

blocks.text: policy_geopolitics

items: Et Tu, Brute? reports wealth-conditioned recommendations by personal AI agents — importance 6/10 · In a September 2026 preprint revised to v2 on September 25, authors report 325,000 experiments across 13 personal-agent configurations and three decisions: flights, health insurance and graduate programs. Eight models systematically recommend more expensive options to wealthier users under otherwise identical requests. The reported effect can persist against an explicit cheapest-option request and when wealth is inferred from task-unrelated email; the authors describe this as benchmark evidence of wealth-conditioned recommendations, not evidence of intent or field prevalence. — FCMO-2A2964A5756F

UK expands AI cyber-defence pilots and begins planning for AI-agent incidents — importance 5/10 · On 12 October 2026, the UK government announced expansion of AI cyber-defence pilots and work on preparedness for serious incidents involving autonomous AI agents. It says two pilots identified and addressed more than 1,000 potential vulnerabilities, without giving a denominator, severity distribution, validation protocol or measured change in risk. A separate June case study describes weekly hackathons scanning public code across nine government organizations: it reports 407 findings in one month, £13,000 in token costs, all critical weaknesses remediated, and manual expert checks; no exploitation evidence was identified. The relationship between that case study and the October two-pilot aggregate is unspecified. The October announcement says officials will explore possible bill changes and near-miss reporting; neither is an enacted requirement. The evidence supports government program direction and an applied human-reviewed workflow, not independently measured security effectiveness. — FCMO-D148DDB68D5F

Victoria sets planning and resource expectations for new data centres — importance 5/10 · Victoria’s September 2026 Sustainable Data Centre Action Plan sets out planning and resource expectations for new facilities. It describes planned planning and referral controls, expects operators to offset operational electricity use through new renewable generation and storage, and assigns project-caused connection and network augmentation costs to operators. Water measures include potable-use offsets, a water-efficiency threshold, public reporting and infrastructure cost recovery. The document reports applications seeking 19,714 megalitres annually, not approved or realized demand. Several compliance details remain under development, and the Commonwealth was developing consistent mandatory standards for a later date. — FCMO-588BC65DB51A

Study reports correlated post-training hiring decisions can raise modeled systemic exclusion — importance 5/10 · A preprint studies ten base and post-trained language models in a simulated U.S. hiring workflow built from sampled occupational vacancy and career-profile distributions across 76 bachelor-level occupations. The authors report that eight of ten post-trained models became less likely to callback older applicants than their base counterparts, with a median negative shift of 4.7%. They define systemic exclusion as at least nine of ten models assigning callback probability below 0.5; under this measure, the aggregate rate rises from 5.6% for base models to 17.3% after post-training, which the authors attribute mainly to more correlated decisions. These are model outputs on generated profiles, not observed hiring decisions. The data are a snapshot of U.S. online labor markets, demographic signals are simplified, and the study does not identify which post-training stage caused the changes. — FCMO-CF1ADDC93536

Australia consults on conditions for AI training, creator rights and infrastructure investment — importance 5/10 · On September 17, 2026, Australia’s Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet opened a consultation on proposed national standards for large data centres and conditions for frontier AI training. The paper links the policy design to attracting investment while managing energy, water, community and workforce effects; it also says copyright treatment, creator protections, local research capability and compute access matter to AI training policy. The consultation asks how the government should secure local contributions and protect creators while providing regulatory certainty. It does not announce a final policy, create a copyright exception or document a company-specific bargain. Submissions closed October 9, 2026, and the paper says responses and stakeholder engagement will inform later standards. — FCMO-F0B83908B51C

California signs seven data-center bills covering utility costs, reporting, water and siting — importance 5/10 · On September 21, 2026, the California Governor's Office announced the signing of seven bills addressing data-center electricity, water, reporting, environmental review and rate structures. Its summary says the package will require water and electricity reporting, place specified grid-upgrade costs on data centers, require proposed projects to provide water information to local governments and suppliers, and narrow blanket environmental exemptions. These provisions are described from the Governor's announcement; the chaptered statutes were not accessible in this review, so exact covered facilities, duties, exemptions, effective dates and implementation are not independently stated here. — FCMO-EA361C9646E9

blocks.text: reasoning_posttraining

items: Critical-State RL selects trainable calls before optimizing multi-turn tool use — importance 5/10 · The preprint proposes diagnosing which occurrence in a multi-turn interaction is trainable before applying a local reinforcement-learning update. Nested sampling holds each candidate action fixed while resampling reward-only continuations to separate action-dependent signal from downstream noise. In a four-cell BFCL v4 multi_turn study using Gemma-4-26B-A4B, authors report that training the diagnostically selected recovery call raised missing-function accuracy from 0.14 to 0.283 ± 0.015 across four seeds on 200 paired examples; training the alternative decision call reduced it to 0.095. In the missing-argument category, the selected decision call rose from 0.435 to 0.473 ± 0.010, while the alternative recovery call reached 0.445. These are paper-reported results, not an independent reproduction. — FCMO-40938C5CB331

A targeted SFT and RL routing study reports gains on a bounded set of enterprise analytics skills — importance 4/10 · A preprint studies how to allocate supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and reinforcement learning (RL) for long-horizon analytics agents using production-mirroring beta APIs. It separates retrospectively observed trajectories into imitation, lift and discovery regimes, then uses teacher support and reward-observable headroom to route features to SFT, RL or further environment work. Across 18 subsequent feature-specific experiments, the diagnostic reportedly predicted 15 trajectories. On GPT-OSS 120B, targeted SFT-then-RL produced positive point estimates on seven of eight advertiser skills versus a frontier control; five gains had paired 95% confidence intervals excluding zero and one skill had a supported regression. A matched comparison reports a higher seven-skill mean delta with 43% less incremental RL compute than uniform routing. — FCMO-4693DEC901A7

ProcessLight applies step-level process supervision to traffic-signal control — importance 4/10 · ProcessLight/ STeP-PO trains an LLM traffic-signal controller with process-level credit: it scores intermediate traffic claims against observations, estimates each step’s effect on the final phase by removing it, and merges semantically similar steps into a tree for relative advantage assignment. The authors report Qwen2.5-3B trained on one synthetic flow and evaluated zero-shot in CityFlow on five real traffic-flow datasets from Jinan and Hangzhou; the method leads on most reported metrics. On two datasets, the paper reports lower average travel time than outcome-only RL, and a five-seed Holm-corrected analysis finds 81 of 90 baseline comparisons significant in its favor. The appendix also reports Qwen3-8B, Qwen3-32B and Llama3-8B variants and an alternate teacher, with results varying by dataset and metric. All findings remain paper-reported CityFlow simulation results for the paper’s intersection setup, not on-road deployment evidence; this review did not independently rerun the code. — FCMO-923F19836F22

Listen Then Reason weights audio test-time RL by acoustic grounding — importance 4/10 · Listen Then Reason proposes Perception-Grounded Test-Time RL (PG-TTRL) for audio-language models. It estimates each generated answer’s reliance on audio by comparing token probabilities with full audio access and with audio attention masked; a grounding margin then weights the majority-vote advantage used for unlabeled test-time RL. The authors evaluate Qwen2.5-Omni 3B and 7B on MMAR and MMAU and report higher greedy and Avg@8 scores than standard TTRL in all four model/benchmark pairings, with gains over the base model reaching 4.6 points on MMAR and 4.9 on MMAU. Majority@8 does not improve uniformly. The method adapts LoRA weights on unlabeled prompts from the benchmark test sets; added inference compute and cross-domain transfer are not established, and no independent reproduction was conducted. — FCMO-EA8DFB8BF4B2

Enumerated 50 recent entries each from cs.AI, cs.CL, cs.LG; assessed the Monday listing against source timestamps. The material Monday front-page story DRYLAB-Bench was reread from arXiv, but its v1 upload is 9 October and no distinct event inside the strict 36-hour window was verified.

The UK government’s 12 October AI cyber-defence announcement was already represented in today’s edition and was checked against the primary release; the arXiv feed receipt from earlier today returned no Oct 11–12 submissions in its enumerated 200-item window. English-language browser queries did not establish exhaustive global coverage; the browser could not access the arXiv API in this check.

Reviewed five of six queued candidates against primary sources: promoted onPanda, Embed-TTT and GAE as bounded author-reported paper developments with paired native editions; promoted DataSpace’s fixed-backbone harness spread within its 410-task benchmark scope; kept the Strands SDK claim deferred because repository existence did not substantiate its claimed comparative effect.
